title: Professor Longhair (Henry Roeland Byrd) Interview, 1978-Fall Transcript

blocks.x: I spoke to Dick Allen about that and he claimed that he didn't have anything like that. Oh! Dick is crazy! He really is because I asked him, you know, I told him what I was interested in doing. And I also talked about WTOL's jazz and he said there's nothing really out in rhythm and blues. He said it's some jazz of course.

Well, for your information, the Jazz Institute at Rutgers University will send you tapes if you request anything. So anything you might want in the way of jazz, you should write to the Jazz Institute at Rutgers. They'll send you tapes. The archives is, you know, is really doing it backwards.
Tony, what do you think would be better? A stationary mic? Should we have a mic stand? Why don't we test?
I'm not going to say anything unless it's ultimately necessary. Okay. I just don't think people want to...
It's alright. Is it turning out okay? Yeah. Okay.
I have a bang chair. Alright.

Fess, something I guess a lot of people, especially those who aren't from New Orleans, would like to know, WTUL having a lot of student listeners who aren't from around here. How did you ever get the name, Professor Longhair?

Well, when I was dancing, of course, when it began, I was dancing. It was called Whirlwind when I was dancing. And I decided to quit dancing and go into the music field. So I left. From up in the direction where I was staying, went across Canal Street, way down around the Seventh-Oo-Six-Wars. People that didn't know me down there, at that time I was wearing long, long hair. And this is where they would approach me, say, Longhair, what is really your name? And I told them my name, but it didn't do any good, because they would still call me Longhair. So I got a job for a fella by the name of Mike Tinsitore. And he was very interested in my music, and he wanted to give me a job, and he accepted it, but he just didn't like the name Longhair. So he changed it to Professor. And them that was calling me Longhair, continually calling me Longhair, and his group was calling me Professor. And finally the names got hooked up together. This is where I became Longhair, so I just kept it. Professor Longhair.

It's funny, the first time I think I saw you was at Tulane, so that's very appropriate. Yeah, we have a little bit of Professor and all. Where'd you grow up, what part of town did you grow up in? Were you, you weren't born in New Orleans, were you?

I was born in Bugaloocy, but my mother brought me here when I was about two months old. And I was born around seven or eight blocks, not born, but I was raised about seven or eight blocks from Canal Street, on the south side. On the south side.
Uh, somebody told me that your mother played piano a lot.
My mother played guitar, drum, bass, piano, harmonica, juice, harp. She also danced and sung. So this is where all my teaching mostly really started from.
So you've been playing as long as you can remember?
As long as I can remember I've been banging and hitting.

Uh, you have a style that's very original to me because it combines, without going to the musical technicalities of it, uh, style elements of marches, a lot of Spanish influences, Caribbean influences, rumbas, boogie woogie. Uh, where does some of that come from? And like, who'd you listen to like when you were growing up?

Well, anything that sounded good to me, whatever attracted me is when I got involved in. And, uh, I listened to, uh, blues, real top blues musicians. I've listened to real top jazz musicians. And I've listened to top Spanish musicians. And sometimes I was involved with them, you know? And so, uh, I practiced these things. Whatever I liked is this, I just started practicing them. And I made a gumbo out of them. I put whatever I wanted together with whatever I needed to support me in my own ideas and what I was doing. Uh, any particular artists? Mmm, no, not really. But, uh, my favorite artists in the blues line was Rocky Sullivan, Stormy Weather, Bertrand, Toots.
Toots is still around.

Brother Montgomery. And now, I was, my favorite right too in Latin beat was Pres, Pres Predon. Maybe we heard of him. Uh, Jazzy, I liked it, uh, I liked it, uh, Jimmy Smith. Yes. Will Doggett. So many people that you take a little bit from each one of these things and, uh, you just, if you know how to do this. Right.
It's simple, you know? You have a gift. Uh, correct me if I'm wrong. I hear a lot of little Brother Montgomery and mess around with some of those things like that. Yeah. A lot, a lot of him.
A lot of his basses, bass work, anyway.
Uh, did you play kind of in a touring group with, going from club to club with Jack Dupree and, uh, somebody told me Red Fox too.

Well, Red Fox didn't play music. Right. He was just a comedian at that time. And we all stuck together back in the 30s, 33, 37, 38, things started to picking up. Uh, this is when I met Jack Dupree around 1937, 38. And he was a comedian also. He sung the blues and he wore union suits out on the stage. Well, at that time I was a one man's band, you know? I did everything. He said, I beat my own drum. I did my own whistling and singing and harmonizing. And I played my own melody. And he wanted to learn to play the piano. And I wanted to really learn to sing, because I wasn't singing too much there, you know? So, a lot of jazz. And this is how I and him got together. And, uh, the first thing he did was, uh, they called them cabbage greens. And I liked it. And this is where I started the singing from that day on. And we sat down to discuss the matter with one another. If he'd teach me what he knew, I'd show him what I know.
Why'd he, uh, leave town? He seems like a...

There wasn't any money to be made here. He tried to get me to go with him when he left. And he came back for me once. But, uh, just somehow I know. I was hooked here, you know? I refused to move. I said if a man could work and satisfy as many people as I was satisfied, I didn't see no reason why I should have to go nowhere else to make a living, you know? That's sort of a lot of...
In them days?
No, I wouldn't go no place. I'd give all the tours away.
It seems pretty sad that, uh, Jack Dupree, he lives in Scandinavia now, somewhere like Sweden. I think so, man.
I haven't run across him. I've always, everywhere I went, he's just been there and left, you know? I haven't saw him in quite a while.

I guess, uh, you've found it kind of difficult. Your popularity's been kind of like a rollercoaster. You've real... Had a lot of, uh, big records in the early 50s and late 40s, and I guess did fairly well in the 50s, and then in the 60s... In the 60s, uh, New Orleans music seems to have taken a really bad turn, and now it seems to be coming back a little bit more interesting.

Well, I was so busy trying to find people that was honest enough to work with, and, uh, I wasn't even keeping up with what the record was doing, because, uh, uh, to my satisfaction, I wasn't getting anything from them, so, to me, it wasn't doing anything, you know? But, uh, around the 70s is where I really adored myself in the music field, because, uh, since I met Allison and them, things began to change, you know? I saw some varied coming, and so this interested me more, of keeping up with where the songs were going to be, you know, exposed.

Were any of the producers back in the 40s and 50s, uh, honest, or any of them good, or were they all... I said Allison. I mean, any of the old, any of the ones from... I said maybe Allison Casper. Just Allison. I don't even want to call the rest of those people the names. Uh, that brings me to another question. One of my favorite songs that you've done is not on an album, uh, an album and such, except it can be found on an English anthology, and that's, uh, your song, Bald Head. Bald Head. How come that's not on an album? Is that tied up in contract with somebody?
No, it's just, I don't know why myself, really, when nobody ever asked.
It's also been recorded. That's right. I think it's gonna be, possibly be on the album that will be coming out within the next year. Yeah.
You're working on an album? New material or old material or both? Well, it's a mix.

It's a mix. Mm-hmm. Uh... But it's much better than it was back in those times, because we have more time to practice now, and really smoothing out your balls, your measurements, you know, instead of just hustling them, you know. There's no feelings. Uh...
Were you ever associated with any of the Indian tribes, or the Mardi Gras Indian tribes? Here in New Orleans or other places?
Yeah.
Anywhere?

Well, I know, uh, Wild Chapitulas, and, uh, Wild Magnolias, and really, we all have rehearsals together. I mean, the Wild Magnolias, we've rehearsed in the same building, from 70 up until about 73, the Indian tribes.
Mm-hmm. And Fess used to let them use his house and his piano for rehearsals when they were preparing for the album. And so they got to know him pretty well. They all live in the same neighborhood.
You're in the Wild Magnolias neighborhood? Yeah. Are they working on a new album?

No, they've split up. Okay, I didn't know. The Wild Chapitulas, I guess, have possibly got another album underway. The Magnolias, uh, as they were, don't exist anymore. It's now separated into two tribes.
Went to, are you saying that some of the Magnolias went?

Some of the Magnolias went one way, and the Golden Eagles, who were always part of the Wild Magnolias. It was a misnomer to begin with because it was always the Golden Eagles and the Wild Magnolias, and it just sounded more romantic, to use one name.

It's kind of like the Wild Chopitulas are now broken, some of them are broken up into the Neville brothers, and they're not exclusive groups. Uh, what song are you happiest with that you've done? Which one do you enjoy playing the most?

The ones that, the new ones. After I play them for about six or seven months, I'm ready to get on something else. It's just the new things that are really interesting to you when you're playing the music.
Uh, what kind of bands do you like to play? What instruments do you like to play?

I wish I could get a full, complete band, it's just, the money ain't there, you know. I need first, second, and third horns. I need all the rhythm sessions. I need congo and bungos. For my Latin and Cuban style of playing.
You'd like to go with the whole big thing like Ray Charles?

Well, I think he's a little too big, I don't think I, well I have mastered it. I've mastered 22 pieces in Big Chief. Uh, what's his name? Uh, the one that arranged for the brass. Wardell Casetta. Wardell Casetta. Wardell Casetta. And that was about the biggest thing I ever did, you know. And it was about 22 pieces and that, all that they did in overdub, you know. It was a live 22 pieces. And since then my mind's been big, you know. I just can't afford it, you know. I wish I could. Right. Yeah, because I can dream of things that, uh, I'd like to create and make happen, you know. But I don't have enough pieces to do it, you know. I need slide and trombone. I need, uh, tenor. I need soprano. I need alto. I need bass, sax. I'm surprised there's a lot of musicians that are jumping the chains to do something. Well.

But you have to have a club, has to be able to support that many musicians. You don't have any clubs in New Orleans if you pay the price that you have to. I mean for recording sessions or something. You still have to pay them. You have to be in the union.

You still have to, you have to teach everybody that I play. It's, it's not the original thing that they hear every day on the box where they can get an acknowledge of what, you know, what should we did and where the changes are.
This is why it's so hard for me to get drummers. Did you, uh, ever go to Cuba or any, I'm trying to get back to, there's so much Latin influence. No, I, no.
You never went to Cuba?
No, I've had a lot of Cubans come to me, you know. Maybe Sunday Castro will have you over there. Uh, is it true that you were once a boxer?
I tried. You tried? Yeah. I boxed for about six months. Cause, I mean, I say boxed, but I mean I was just in the game because the first night I got whipped I quit, you know.
My grandfather had the same thing happen to him. Yeah, I couldn't take it. It was nice issuing it out. Uh, what sort of, uh, plans or hopes do you have like for the future?
Ah, making my grandchildren as happy as I possibly can. I imagine I'll get a lot of enjoyment out of that. I didn't get too old to execute what's in my mind, you know.
And you are working on a new album. All the time I'll be working on it. Do you think you'll record that here in New Orleans or? I think I will.
Yeah, do you think it'll be recorded here? All this is left up to me in the castle. I don't worry about the business end of the situation. I just like to get the groups in.
We recorded an album on Marty's right, Tipitina's. Uh huh. That will be coming out within the next year.
it's live, it's in the team.
Great. How do you...
Put out live albums or studio albums, live.
How do you like having a bar named after one of your songs?
Oh, it makes you feel great. We could get a few more, you know. Then we could really support the group, you know.
Do you think artists are being better treated in general today than they were a couple of years ago?

Much better from the side that I see it. Some of them are still getting roughed up, you know. Like I see, it's the honesty and the person that's handling your affairs that makes your business what it is because all along they should have been getting treated real swell. But some of them bring things against themselves. I can only speak for myself. It's swell with me, you know.
Who are some of the musicians you've enjoyed playing with over the years?
The group that I have now.
People like Jesse Hill, I think you...
Well... Did you ever play with him? Yeah, we wait together from 49 until around 50. And he left, went to California.
Did you ever go... I heard that there was like a New Orleans club of musicians over in the West Coast. Did you ever go out there and play with them at all? I didn't appreciate them.
I went out there to play with them. I don't think they was too friendly, you know.
I heard they had to play things like go-go joints and things like that. Right, right.
Stayed for it as you know what's not to make it. I didn't enjoy them kind of things. I enjoyed making people happy.
When you first started playing, and I guess through the early 60s, were there a lot of racial barriers?
I never was bothered with it myself. I mean I've been playing with mixed groups and mixed houses all my life. I was raised up with white people to tell you the truth of them.
So New Orleans has always been better than I guess some areas in that respect.
Yeah, I've never had any trouble with races. Only here lately, since the 70s when I started going down in Chalamet part of town. Those people don't like nobody.
Excuse me?
Can we cover Chalamet or...?
We go after Chalamet. They're kind of rough down there. They're pretty rough on us when we don't play their requests.
Oh yeah.

Yeah, they're rough. I'm going to ask you about one song. And you don't have to answer this if you don't feel like it. Somebody wanted me to ask you this. Is Ball of the Wall a dance? Does it mean something else? How did you come up with that?

The people came up with that. Since they've been calling Ball of the Wall, I've been trying to memorize myself where it really is. I don't remember no song I ever made by the name of Ball of the Wall, but I might have said Ball of the Wall in some of the things I was doing. And they took it for granted that was the title of the song. Now I do say Ballie, Ballie, Ballie, Ballie, Wallie. But that's when she walks right in and she walks right out. That's the title of the song. Sometimes I'll be singing the song. She walks right in and she walks right out and she says Ball of the Wall. They're still hollering for Ball. I don't know, you know, really.
Well I think the Atlantic record, the reissue, has Ball of the Wall on it. It's, uh, we're going to have a little fun with you all. Oh, yeah.
Yeah. Yeah, but now those songs weren't supposed to have been released. It never was finished, you know?

Yeah, these were, sometimes they were, kept the machines running and Fest was just working things out, you know. And that album in particular has a lot of previously unissued material and it wasn't supposed to be issued. It was just a practice run.

You can tell it because the beginnings are really abrupt and the endings just kind of, there's no fade out. They just go and they're off. I was wondering whether Ball of the Wall might have even come from when you were dancing and someone told me, people, there used to be style dancing where people would almost dance up the walls a little bit, like tap dancing or something. I was wondering. Well, that's when I used to dance.

I used to run up the wall and back down, but there wasn't no Ball of the Wall in the box in there. It's just things we'd be sketching and going over feeling good and happy and they were still recording the stuff. It shouldn't have never been put out because it never was completed.
What was the very first song that you did that was recorded?

Well, Ball Head was one in Mardi Gras, New Orleans. And we came out trying to please the people, please the women that had Ball Head rather. It was hearing our baby hearing our honey child. And on the other side I think it was in the night at that time.

One of my, another favorite song of mine that you do is Blues Rumba. Is that one that you like? Is your Blues Rumba instrumental. It's on that Atlantic album. Is that one that you ever mentioned? There's another one that shouldn't have been released.
Incomplete.
It's beautiful to me. But you still consider it incomplete. It's amazing. I think that's about it. Is there anything you'd like to say to the audience or anything you'd like to get into?
I'm just telling them to stay happy and keep your chin up. We'll stand by on the 1010 listening in. Hope to meet them and greet them soon.
Are you going to be, are you going to be playing around town in the, in the near future, continuing to?
We're supposed to play on the 14th.

He's doing the benefit for the Academy of Black Arts on the 14th. And the 15th will be at the Superdome for the Ali fight. And then 16th Tipitinas. But generally we play at Tipitinas regularly. That's, that's the place that's best as home. And that's the place people should come here and really. And the rest of the time we, the travel, well, you know, we just got back from Europe this summer, which was very exciting in Scandinavia. And they plan on having him back in March. So.

Fess, let me ask you one more question. One more question. So many of the albums even of New Orleans music come out in England and France and some in Germany. Do you have any feeling as to why people over there sometimes seem to be more aware of music that's going on here than even the people in New Orleans?

No, I haven't been able to figure that out. I know more than that. The people over there seem to appreciate more than the people here, you know. People here just want to get, well, I don't want to say what's in my mind. If they can't get a drink or be out with a girlfriend, it is assuming they don't come in, you know. That's not really interested in the music. You just want to go someplace, you know. Look how people go for jazz here. They love it. But now you let a jazz band go down an auditorium or the super don't. You see about three people in the house, you know. So, you got nothing. You know. People just talk. They don't patronize. I don't think I, if it don't be for the people at Tip of 10 that we have here among friends, their friends. And their friends, it'd be nothing, you know. People don't care too much about music here.

I think it's a question of authenticity and I think that the Europeans have a great appreciation for American culture. And the Americans have a great appreciation for popular culture. So, you know, it's a question of, they want to know what, they want to know about the history of New Orleans music, all the way from traditional jazz and of course blues. And the tremendous fascination with all kinds of artists that are totally obscured here. So, Bess just satisfies that need for them. And he represents New Orleans as well as blues. And as well as the great piano tradition in America.

Yeah, that's certainly true. Because when I was in England, people always asking me about it. They found out I was from New Orleans. They always ask me about it. Do you mind it when people like, talk a lot? When you play, I've noticed this not so much when you play because people dance a lot. But I've been in certain clubs that won't come mention here where people, as you say, they're there for, to drink or, I don't know, impress whoever they're with. And they don't really listen to musicians. Does all that noise distract you a lot? I never look out there.

You're always watching that. I've always watched my keyboard or the men's on the bed. I never look out in the audience because it's too much to distract your attention and make you feel real, you know, down. It gets you, pull you down. Some people will sit down and it's like, you know, and you be working and working and you're building up sweat and everything. You're trying to, you know, pat the feet or anything or clap the hands or applaud. But then you sit there, you know. Now, the only way to beat that is to don't pay them people no mind. Work. Do the best you can. Enjoy yourselves when they get like that out there. Because people can embrace you, you know.

All right. Well, thank you very much. And we'll be definitely coming to see you soon. Thank you very much. Why don't we play some of the facts that turned out. It is amazing. I've seen. I don't know. What do you think? That's a great idea. This is, uh, let's see. This is Professor Long here. You're listening to the, it's clear through all the symptoms.
I haven't really, you know, notated the date and everything on here, but this is the, and I have to tape it together. We're gonna, I'll give you a press kit. Would you like one? Yes, I really would.
I don't know. I don't know. I don't know. I don't know. Something like, uh, this is Professor Long here. If you want to hear some fine music, listen to WTUL. Anything along those lines.
This is Professor Long here. And if you want to listen to some fine music, listen to WTUL. Okay, true. Good.

segments.title: Opening chatter and microphone setup
segments.summary: Crawford talks about WTUL's rhythm and blues holdings, SPEAKER_03 mentions Rutgers jazz tapes, and they test the mic.

segments.title: How he got the name Professor Longhair
segments.summary: He explains that he danced as Whirlwind, kept long hair, and bandleader Mike Tessitore added Professor, so the names merged.

segments.title: Born in Bogalusa, raised in New Orleans, mother's music
segments.summary: Born elsewhere, brought to New Orleans at two months, raised near Canal Street; his mother played many instruments and was his first teacher.

segments.title: His blended style and favorite musicians
segments.summary: He describes mixing blues, jazz and Latin sounds into a gumbo and names favorites like Little Brother Montgomery, Perez Prado, Jimmy Smith and Bill Doggett.

segments.chapter: Early partnerships and career ups and downs
segments.title: Champion Jack Dupree and Redd Foxx in the late 1930s
segments.summary: He met comedian-singer Jack Dupree around 1937-38; they traded piano for singing lessons. Dupree later left town and Fess refused to leave.

segments.chapter: Early partnerships and career ups and downs
segments.title: Records, honest producers, the 1970s turn and Bald Head
segments.summary: He talks about not following his records, the change after meeting Allison in the 1970s, and the unreleased Bald Head and the upcoming album.

segments.title: Mardi Gras Indians rehearsing at his house
segments.summary: He rehearsed alongside the Wild Magnolias and Wild Tchoupitoulas; SPEAKER_03 explains the tribes' split.

segments.title: Which songs he enjoys playing
segments.summary: He prefers new songs and tires of them after six or seven months.

segments.title: Wanting a full band; the 22-piece Big Chief session
segments.summary: He wishes he could afford horns and Latin percussion; recalls the live 22-piece Big Chief recording; cost and teaching the parts are obstacles.

segments.title: Cuba, brief boxing, and hopes for the future
segments.summary: He never went to Cuba, boxed briefly, and hopes to make his grandchildren happy.

segments.title: New album, live recording at Tipitina's, bar named for his song
segments.summary: A new album will probably be recorded in New Orleans; a live Tipitina's album is coming; he likes having a bar named after his song.

segments.title: Are artists treated better today
segments.summary: He says treatment is much better but depends on honest handlers.

segments.title: Playing with Jesse Hill and the West Coast New Orleans musicians
segments.summary: He played with Jesse Hill 1949-50 and visited the West Coast musicians' scene, which he did not enjoy.

segments.title: Racial barriers and rough Chalmette audiences
segments.summary: He says he never had racial trouble with mixed groups until the 1970s in Chalmette.

segments.title: Origin of the title Ball of the Wall and the unreleased session
segments.summary: He says audiences coined the title; the Atlantic reissue includes unfinished practice recordings that were never meant for release.

segments.title: First recorded song and Blues Rumba
segments.summary: He mentions Bald Head as his first recording, and Blues Rumba as another incomplete track that was released.

segments.title: Message to listeners and upcoming gigs
segments.summary: He greets listeners; SPEAKER_03 lists a benefit, the Superdome Ali fight, Tipitina's, and the return from Europe.

segments.title: Why Europeans appreciate New Orleans music more; audience noise
segments.summary: Fess and SPEAKER_03 explain European appreciation; he says he ignores distracting audiences and watches his keyboard.

segments.title: Wrap-up, press kit and station ID
segments.summary: Thanks, a press kit offer, and a WTUL station ID recording.
